genZNote: Not a bacterium at all — it's an archaeon living in the human gut, quietly converting hydrogen and CO2 into methane so your other gut microbes can work more efficiently.

morphology.notes: An archaeon, not a bacterium — has a distinct cell wall (pseudopeptidoglycan) and unique archaeal membrane lipids; not meaningfully described by the bacterial Gram stain.

habitat.hostAssociation: The dominant archaeal member of the normal human gut microbiome in most people who harbor detectable methanogens
habitat.environmentalOccurrence: Found almost exclusively within mammalian/human GI tracts, not free-living in soil or water

microscopy.stain: Not Gram-stained in routine practice; identified via specialized anaerobic culture or molecular methods

culture.media: Specialized strict-anaerobic methanogen media (rarely performed in clinical labs)
culture.growthCharacteristics: Strict anaerobe; uses hydrogen and CO2 (or formate) to produce methane

identificationClues: An archaeon, not a bacterium — belongs to an entirely separate domain of life with distinct cell wall chemistry and membrane lipids
Consumes hydrogen produced by fermenting gut bacteria and converts it, with CO2, into methane — helping maintain efficient fermentation by other gut microbes
Strict anaerobe, essentially never encountered outside the mammalian GI tract
Its abundance correlates with breath methane production, used clinically in some breath testing for GI motility/SIBO evaluation

examFacts.importantTest: Breath methane testing reflects its metabolic activity
examFacts.distinguishingFeature: The dominant archaeon of the human gut microbiome, illustrating that not every gut microbe is a bacterium

sources.name: NCBI Bookshelf — overview of the human gut microbiome and methanogenic archaea
